title: Ischemic Stroke in Bacterial Meningitis: A Multicentric Retrospective Cohort Study
summary:
Bacterial meningitis is a severe infection of the membranes surrounding the brain that can still be life-threatening despite antibiotic treatment. In roughly one in five patients, the inflammation spreads to the blood vessels of the brain and causes a stroke. These patients face a considerably higher risk of dying or of being left with permanent disability. At present there is no specific treatment to prevent such strokes.
In this study, the medical records of adult patients treated for bacterial meningitis at the university hospitals in Lübeck and Kiel are analysed. The study examines how often strokes occur, at which point during the illness they occur, which brain regions are affected, and which factors are associated with their occurrence. No additional examinations or burdens arise for the patients — only data already collected during routine treatment are analysed.
The aim is to better understand when and why these strokes develop. This may in future help to identify approaches for detecting or preventing them in time.

interventions.name: Retrospective analysis of all adult patients diagnosed with and treated for community-acquired bacterial meningitis between 01/2010 and 06/2026, with regard to the occurrence of ischemic stroke.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Community-acquired bacterial meningitis (clinical signs AND cerebrospinal fluid white blood cell count > 1,000/µl and/or detection of a bacterial pathogen in the cerebrospinal fluid), treated as inpatients at one of the participating centres during the observation period.
Exclusion criteria:
Tuberculous meningitis; immunocompromised state (e.g. HIV infection, solid organ or haematopoietic cell transplantation); recent neurosurgical procedure.
